explanation: Posterior external arcuate fibers connect the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Anterior external arcuate fibers relay in the arcuate nucleus of the opposite side before projecting to the cerebellum.
Arcuate fibers (both internal and external) carry proprioceptive impulses from the body to the cerebellum and brainstem nuclei.
Internal arcuate fibers arise from the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the medulla, cross at the sensory decussation, and form the medial lemniscus.
The medial lemniscus originates from the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side after their fibers cross (internal arcuate fibers).
Decussation of internal arcuate fibers (sensory decussation) occurs in the upper part of the closed medulla, at the level of the olivary nuclei.
First order proprioceptive neurons have large cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia with thick myelinated fibers that give off ascending and descending branches in the posterior column.
Astrocytes form the blood-brain barrier through their foot processes surrounding CNS capillaries, regulating molecular passage into the brain.
The ventral vestibulospinal tract passes in the medial longitudinal bundle, coordinating head position and eye movements.
The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve contains first order neurons for proprioception from the face, the only case of sensory neurons in the CNS.
First order neurons for pain and temperature from the face have cell bodies in the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion, with central processes entering the spinal nucleus.
Second order neurons for simple touch from the face are in the main (principal) sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve.
The trigeminal lemniscus (trigeminothalamic tract) is present in the medulla and pons, carrying facial sensory information to the VPM thalamus.
The medial geniculate body contains the final neurons of the auditory pathway, projecting via the acoustic radiation to the primary auditory cortex.
The arachnoid barrier cell layer separates extracerebral capillaries from the subarachnoid space, contributing to the blood-CSF barrier.
Tight junctions between ependymal cells form the blood-CSF barrier at the ventricular surface, along with choroid plexus epithelium.
The blood-brain barrier uses tight junctions between non-fenestrated (continuous) capillary endothelial cells, unlike fenestrated endothelium elsewhere.
Border cells (meningothelial cells) are found in the arachnoid mater, forming a continuous layer adjacent to the dura.
Pia mater is formed of modified fibroblasts (mesothelial cells), a single layer that closely invests the brain and spinal cord surface.
Each climbing fiber forms powerful excitatory synapses with multiple Purkinje cell dendrites; one Purkinje cell receives input from a single climbing fiber.
Stereognosis (recognition of objects by touch) requires intact dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway; cuneate tract carries this from the upper limb.
In meningitis, inflamed meninges become more permeable allowing increased penicillin entry; normal BBB restricts many antibiotics from CNS.
Lesion of the right gracile nucleus impairs fine touch and stereognosis on the right lower limb (ipsilateral) because the gracile tract is already ipsilateral.
Posterior column lesion at lumbar level causes loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception (tactile discrimination) in the ipsilateral lower limbs.
Syringomyelia damages crossing spinothalamic fibers causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature in a cape-like distribution over upper limbs and chest.
The trigeminal lemniscus carries all sensory modalities from one side of the face; lesion causes contralateral facial sensory loss.
Tabes dorsalis (dorsal column degeneration in neurosyphilis) causes sensory ataxia due to loss of proprioception, leading to gait problems.
The lateral ventricle is the only cavity in the telencephalon, with anterior horn in frontal lobe, body in parietal, and posterior/temporal horns in temporal lobe.
The third ventricle has choroid plexus in its roof (derived from tela choroidea) producing CSF; lateral ventricles also have choroid plexus.
Choroid plexus is formed by a capillary network (from pia) covered by a thin layer of cuboidal epithelial cells (modified ependyma).
The fourth ventricle roof is formed by the superior cerebellar peduncle (superior medullary velum) and inferior medullary velum, not the floor.
The optic tract is a content of the interpeduncular fossa, carrying visual information from the optic chiasma to the lateral geniculate body.
The optic tract forms the lateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa; the cerebral peduncles form the posterior boundary.
Olfactory nerve filaments from the nasal mucosa synapse in the olfactory bulb, which then projects via the olfactory tract to cortical areas.
The trigeminal nerve (CN V) contains sensory fibers for face, scalp, and oral cavity; the other listed nerves are purely motor.
